title: Repeated String Match
statement:
You are given two strings `a` and `b`. Repeating `a` means writing it several times one after another: repeating `"ab"` three times gives `"ababab"`.

Find the **minimum** number of times `a` must be repeated so that `b` appears in the result as a contiguous substring. If no number of repetitions makes `b` a substring, return `-1`.

Note that `b` may be shorter than `a`, in which case a single copy of `a` may already be enough.

**Follow-up:** Start from the brute-force approach (build the repeated string and search it), improve the search to KMP, and then solve the substring search again with a Rabin-Karp rolling hash. Discuss when hash collisions matter.
inputFormat:
The first line contains the string `a`.
The second line contains the string `b`.
outputFormat: Print a single integer: the minimum number of repetitions of `a`, or `-1` if `b` can never be a substring.
constraints: `a` and `b` consist of lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: Three copies give `abcabcabc` (length 9), which has no substring `cabcabca` because it would need to start at index 2 and end at index 9. Four copies give `abcabcabcabc`, which contains `cabcabca` starting at index 2.
One copy `xyz` is too short. Two copies `xyzxyz` contain `yzxy` starting at index 1.
In any repetition of `abc`, the letter after `a` is always `b`, so `ac` never occurs.

hints: If `b` fits inside some repetition of `a` at all, how many copies of `a` can you possibly need? Think about where an occurrence of `b` could start inside the first copy.
Repeat `a` just enough times that its length is at least |b| + |a|, then search for `b` once. The answer follows from the end position of the first occurrence.
Use a linear-time search (KMP failure function or a rolling hash) so that the search itself does not cost O(|a| * |b|).
